references.text: In the preceding verse ([ref:Luk 23:5|Luke 23:5]), the Jews accuse Jesus of stirring up the people "from Galilee all the way here." It is this mention of Galilee that causes Pilate to ask whether Jesus is a Galilean.
Pilate's question about whether Jesus was a Galilean leads directly to him sending Jesus to Herod Antipas, who had jurisdiction over Galilee ([ref:Luk 23:7|Luke 23:7]).
Although Jesus was born in Bethlehem in Judea ([ref:Luk 2:4|Luke 2:4]), he grew up in Nazareth in Galilee, which explains why he was regarded as a Galilean.
Jesus began his public ministry in Galilee ([ref:Luk 4:14|Luke 4:14]) and became known as the Galilean.
Joseph settled with his family in Nazareth in Galilee ([ref:Matt 2:22-23|Matthew 2:22-23]), which gave Jesus the connection to Galilee that Pilate asks about.
People referred to Jesus as "the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee" ([ref:Matt 21:11|Matthew 21:11]), and this was the common understanding of his origin.
Some objected that Christ could not come from Galilee ([ref:Joh 7:41|John 7:41]), showing that Jesus' Galilean background was a known and debated topic.
The Pharisees rejected the idea that a prophet could come from Galilee ([ref:Joh 7:52|John 7:52]), which highlights the same identification that Pilate asks about.
In [ref:Joh 18:29|John 18:29], Pilate goes out to the Jews and asks what they accuse Jesus of, paralleling the trial here in Luke where Pilate examines the charges more closely.
After the resurrection, the disciples are addressed as "men from Galilee" ([ref:Apg 1:11|Acts 1:11]), showing that the connection to Galilee continued to characterize Jesus' followers.
